Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Sustainability
Combining data-driven learning with physical laws to build more reliable, interpretable models for environmental and engineering challenges.
MACHINE LEARNING
SUSTAINABILITY
ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE

What is Physics-Informed Machine Learning?
Traditional ML learns only from historical data — for example, temperature and humidity inputs mapped to predicted air pollution. But environmental data is often limited, noisy, or expensive to collect.
PIML = Data-driven learning + Physics-based constraints
Traditional ML
Data → Model → Prediction
Physics-Informed ML
Data + Physical Laws → Model → Physically Consistent Prediction

Why PIML for Sustainability?
Sustainability systems are governed by physical processes. A purely data-driven model may produce unrealistic predictions when conditions fall outside the training data. PIML embeds physical knowledge to reduce this risk.
Domain | Governing Physics
Climate | Atmospheric and ocean dynamics
Air Pollution | Pollutant transport and diffusion
Water Resources | Fluid flow and hydrology
Solar Energy | Radiation and energy conversion
Agriculture | Soil-water-plant interactions
Batteries | Electrochemical behaviour
Groundwater | Subsurface flow

How Does PIML Work?
Final Prediction
Apply Physics Penalty
Train Model
Identify Laws
Collect Data
The key insight: the model is not just minimising prediction error — it is also penalised when its output violates known physical behaviour. The result is a prediction that is both data-faithful and physically plausible.

PIML Across Sustainability Domains
Climate & Weather
Atmospheric dynamics embedded into ML improves extreme-weather forecasting, climate-risk assessment, and disaster preparedness.
Energy Systems
Solar and wind forecasting benefit from irradiance and aerodynamic constraints, enabling better grid stability and renewable integration.
Agriculture
Soil-water-plant physics combined with sensor data enables precise irrigation decisions, reducing water waste and crop stress.
Environmental Monitoring
Sparse sensor networks are augmented with pollutant transport physics to produce reliable air and water quality maps.

PIML vs Traditional Approaches
A Simple Way to Think About It
Traditional ML
"Learn from what has happened."
Physics-Based Modelling
"Use what we know about how the system works."
Physics-Informed ML
"Learn from observations while respecting what we know about how the system works."

PIML and Digital Twins
A digital twin represents a physical system digitally. PIML becomes a powerful engine within the twin, combining sensor observations, physical simulation, and learned patterns.

The Big Picture: PIML for Sustainable Action
Climate
Weather observations + atmospheric physics → extreme-weather prediction → disaster preparedness
Energy
Solar/wind data + energy physics → renewable generation forecast → grid optimisation
Agriculture
Soil/crop/weather data + water physics → irrigation prediction → water conservation
Environment
Sensor/satellite data + pollutant transport → pollution mapping → environmental management

Challenges & Case Study
Key Challenges
Correct physical model
Incorrect assumptions can degrade performance
Computational complexity
Training is more demanding than conventional ML
Balancing data and physics
Weighting   requires careful tuning
Data quality
Noise, gaps, and calibration errors persist
Case Study: Smart Irrigation
A farm uses soil-moisture sensors, weather data, and satellite imagery. PIML combines these with water-flow and evapotranspiration physics to predict crop water requirements.
Outcome: Reduced water consumption, lower pumping energy, less crop stress — balancing productivity with conservation.
